label: E8_environment_probe
status: HISTORICAL / SUPERSEDED -- captured 2026-08-04 19:07 JST, while this host's GPU was still occupied by a resident vLLM server (~23.8/24.5 GB VRAM used, ~305 MiB free). The GPU was freed shortly afterward (vLLM stopped, ~23.5 GB became free) and E8a-E8e were successfully re-run against real GPU compute -- see e8a_run*.json / e8b_run*.json / e8c_cpu_vs_gpu.json / e8d_tf32.json / e8_ulp_diff.json for the current, successful results, and the README's 'GPU実験(E8系)' section for the analysis. This file is kept purely as a record of that first (blocked) attempt and the root-cause investigation into it -- it does NOT describe the current state of the GPU or the current experiment results.
note: Not one of the compare.py-driven experiments; a standalone record of the root-cause investigation into why every E8a-E8d GPU measurement failed with a CUDA OOM at the time, done before the GPU was freed. Kept here so the article author has the exact evidence (not just a paraphrase) without having to re-run diagnostics, and so the 'GPU実験がVRAM枯渇でブロックされた' episode itself remains documented as part of the experiment history.

host_nvidia_smi.sampled_5_times_over_10s: stable at used=23768 free=305 across all samples
host_nvidia_smi.resident_process: vLLM::EngineCore (PID varies), ~23172 MiB; a second /usr/bin/python process holds ~564 MiB
host_nvidia_smi.instruction_compliance: neither process was touched/killed, per task constraints

bare_cuda_c_test.purpose: rule out a PyTorch-specific bug by testing raw CUDA driver/runtime behavior directly, with no PyTorch/cuDNN/cuBLAS involved
bare_cuda_c_test.interpretation: the driver cannot even establish a CUDA context (let alone allocate a 1MB buffer) with only 305 MiB of free VRAM on this RTX 4090. This is a genuine, reproducible resource-exhaustion condition at the CUDA driver level, not a container/toolkit/PyTorch compatibility problem.

pytorch_lightweight_probe.purpose: determine which torch.cuda.* calls need a live CUDA context/allocation vs which are safe metadata-only queries, so E8 scripts could still collect rich environment metadata even though real GPU compute is blocked
failed_with_cuda_oom: torch.cuda.mem_get_info() -> RuntimeError: CUDA error: out of memory
torch.zeros(1, device='cuda') -> RuntimeError: CUDA error: out of memory (even a single float32 element)
pytorch_lightweight_probe.conclusion: torch.cuda.is_available() returning True is NOT sufficient evidence that GPU compute will actually work when VRAM is this tight -- it only reflects driver/device visibility, not whether a context can be created. This distinction is worth stating explicitly in the article, since it contradicts the naive assumption that 'is_available() == True' implies GPU experiments are runnable.

conclusion_for_e8: Every E8a/E8b/E8c/E8d measurement that needs any CUDA tensor allocation fails identically with RuntimeError: CUDA error: out of memory, at every fallback size down to a single element, in every one of the 3+3 repeated containers. This is expected given the above: the GPU has only ~305 MiB free (vLLM holds ~23.8/24.5 GB), and even a bare CUDA context needs more than that. The E8 scripts and run_gpu.sh are fully implemented and were run to completion; what they demonstrate in this environment is that the failure itself is perfectly reproducible (identical error message, 0 mismatches across repeated containers in e8a_compare_*.json / e8b_compare_*.json), while the metadata-only fields (GPU name/capability/cuDNN version/TF32 defaults) were successfully collected throughout.
